cards.explanation: The answer is first. Paul says, "On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up…" (1 Corinthians 16:2). The reason he gives is "…so that when I come no collections will be needed." A little at a time, every week. That's a plan even I could stick to, friends, and I once forgot a whole batch in the oven.

The answer is people the Corinthians recommend. Paul says, "…I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem." (1 Corinthians 16:3). So the Corinthians do the recommending, and Paul sends letters along with the ones they recommend. I like that, friends. The Corinthians get a say in who goes.

The answer is Jerusalem. Paul says the people the Corinthians recommend will "…carry your gift to Jerusalem." (1 Corinthians 16:3). That's the destination for the gift for the saints. Jerusalem is easy to remember and hard to say with a mouthful of cookie, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says, "And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me." (1 Corinthians 16:4). Notice the "if." Paul leaves it open, and he doesn't say he's definitely going. If it works out, they all travel together.

The answer is that he hopes they will help him on his journey wherever he goes. Paul says he may stay awhile, or even spend the winter, "…so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go." (1 Corinthians 16:6). That's the hope he states. A good visit, and then a send-off with a little help for the road.

The answer is if the Lord permits. Paul says, "I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits." (1 Corinthians 16:7). He makes his plans and he holds them with open hands. I like that, friends. I plan my batches the same way.

The answer is False. Paul says, "…a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me." (1 Corinthians 16:9). So there is opposition, and he stays anyway. A great door and many opponents, side by side in one verse.

The answer is that he is doing the work of the Lord like Paul. Paul says to see to it that Timothy has nothing to fear, "…for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am." (1 Corinthians 16:10). That's the reason in the text. Timothy's work is the same work Paul is doing.

The answer is contempt. Paul says, "No one, then, should treat him with contempt." (1 Corinthians 16:11). Contempt is looking down on someone, and Paul says don't do it. He follows that with sending Timothy off in peace. I've been looked down on in a junk drawer, friends, and I wouldn't wish it on a guest.

The answer is False. Paul says, "Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers." (1 Corinthians 16:11). He's expecting Timothy back, so the Corinthians are to send him off, not keep him. A good host knows when to wave goodbye.

The answer is not now, but he'll go when he has the chance. Paul says Apollos "…was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity." (1 Corinthians 16:12). So it's a not now, with a promise of later. Paul asked strongly and still left room for Apollos' answer. I'd say that's how a good friend handles a no for now.

The answer is converts. Paul says Stephanas and his household "…were the first converts in Achaia…" (1 Corinthians 16:15). They were the first people there to believe. Then Paul says they "…have devoted themselves to the service of the saints." First in line and still serving.

The answer is to submit to them and every fellow worker. Paul urges the brothers "…to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer." (1 Corinthians 16:16). So the call goes beyond Stephanas's household to every fellow worker and laborer. The people who serve are the ones worth following. I'd follow anybody who has been up since dawn doing the dishes.

The answer is refreshed. Paul says, "For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well." (1 Corinthians 16:18). So Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus did good for Paul and for the Corinthians too. Some people walk in and the whole room gets lighter. A fresh batch of cookies does the same thing for me, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says, "Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men." (1 Corinthians 16:18). They refreshed his spirit and the Corinthians', so appreciation is the answer he gives. A thank-you goes a long way, friends. Nobody ever told me no to a thank-you.

The answer is True. Paul says, "Greet one another with a holy kiss." (1 Corinthians 16:20). It comes right after the brothers with him send their greetings. That's how he tells them to greet each other. A warm hello, and it's in the text.

The answer is the grace of the Lord Jesus and Paul's own love. Paul closes with, "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you." Then he adds, "My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen." (1 Corinthians 16:23-24). Grace first, then his own love for all of them. That's a warm way to end a letter, even with a hard line earlier in the closing.
